demand_source.title: Text-to-speech configuration
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw documents local speech engines on a Mac as a supported way to turn replies into audio.

caveats: iMessage is not a voice-note channel: the reply is an audio file attachment, not a voice bubble. The voice-bubble option (`asVoice` on upload-file) belongs to the Private API action set, which needs SIP off.
Local engines emit WAV, so a few minutes of speech is several megabytes.
Long replies are summarized by the chat model before synthesis (a cloud call) or truncated.
Two tempting shortcuts are cloud services and must stay off for kids' content: the no-key Microsoft provider (Edge online TTS) and the bundled `sag` skill (ElevenLabs).
The built-in `tts` tool only speaks when asked, which is the right default: nobody wants every text reply doubled as audio.

Local-only is not the default. The keyless Microsoft provider is enabled by default, and the docs say other configured providers act as fallbacks, so a stopped local server could end in a cloud call unless Microsoft is disabled.

`/tts provider <id>` is open to any authorized sender and writes one preference file on the gateway host, so a single text can move speech to another provider for everyone. Having no cloud provider configured is the control; a prompt rule is not.

Option A adds a third-party Homebrew package and a long-running loopback server under the happy user, plus a model download: an install, a launch agent, a firewall rule and a one-time egress exception.
The loopback route needs Speech Swift v0.0.23 or later. It is a 0.0.x project, so pin the version and expect rough edges; the server also needs its own launchd job to stay up.
None of `speech`, `speech-server` or `ffmpeg` is installed on this Mac today.
iMessage outbound media is capped by `channels.imessage.mediaMaxMb` (default 16 MB), which bounds the length of a WAV reply.
In the car the phone already does the speaking: Siri announces Happy's text replies, so no audio file is needed there.
edits.safety: Speech synthesis is an output transformation on the gateway host and adds no new way for an agent to send data out. It is local-only, and so usable for kids' content later, only after the cloud speech providers are disabled in config and blocked at the proxy; the default provider chain and the provider slash command would otherwise allow a cloud voice. Long replies pass through a summary model before synthesis, which must be local or off for kids. Keep provider switching by directive off (the voice guardrails now recorded under VOX-01).

edits.description: A handful of typed commands that already work in the iMessage thread: stop an answer that is going wrong, start a clean conversation, see what Happy can do right now, and check health and cost, all handled before any model call. One more does use the model: /btw asks a side question that is not remembered (its page does not list iMessage, so treat it as untested here).

edits.how: Text commands are core and work on iMessage: command-only messages from allowlisted senders are handled before the queue and the model. /stop aborts the active run in that chat; /new archives the session and starts fresh; /tools lists the agent's effective tools; /status shows runtime, uptime and plugin health; /usage tokens|full|cost toggles a per-reply footer or prints a cost summary. /btw answers from the current session with a separate one-shot model query and writes nothing to history. Put the five everyday ones in templates/person/AGENTS.md and a one-screen cheat sheet. The config-writing commands stay off as today, and Tony should decide whether /restart and /update, which one switch (commands.restart, on by default) opens to owners, stay available from chat.
depends_on: G005 kill switch for the stop-everything case
caveats: /stop ends one run in one chat; it does not pause scheduled jobs, so it complements the G005 kill phrase rather than replacing it.
The /btw page names WhatsApp, Telegram and Discord for channel use and does not mention iMessage.
/btw is a separate one-shot model call on the session's model; it is not free and not model-less.
/usage figures are local estimates, not the provider's bill.
In a plain iMessage bubble the /status and /tools output may be long.

/loop is left off the cheat sheet. It is an owner-only command that has the agent create a repeating job through the scheduling tool, so it does nothing until F007 grants that tool, and a job made this way sits outside the G003 jobs registry. Its prerequisites and house rule are recorded with the multi-day project entry (AUT-01); a loop on a parent's agent sees only search snippets, so watching a page or a feed belongs to the watchers (F029).

demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's built-in page fetcher gets a URL and returns its readable text, which is what lets the helper answer from a public page.

edits.safety: The research agent reads untrusted pages but holds no memory, no accounts and no family data, and the guardrails take the home network out of its reach. That keeps private data away from the agent that browses; it does not close every path. The guardrails do not stop an injected page making the helper request some public URL, and the roadmap names the hand-off as the one remaining leak path: the parent's agent holds memory, reads search results, attachments and the helper's relayed answer, and writes the task text that goes to a helper able to fetch any public address. OpenClaw's guidance is to deny sessions_spawn by default to an agent that handles outside content (tool-permissions.md:21), so this grant is deliberate and narrow: the allowlist names only research, the rule about what may go into the task text is a prompt rule, and the roadmap's exit test includes an injected result that asks the parent's agent to pass memory to research. The relayed answer is treated as untrusted.
